title: OPPOSITION: San Marzano No. 2 (003209031)
text:
OPPOSITION Nо B 3 209 031

Consorzio di tutela del pomodoro S. Marzano Dell'Qgro Sarnese-Nocerino, Via Lanzara, 27, 84087 Sarno (SA), Italy (opponent), represented by G.D. Di Grazia D'Alto & C.S.N.C., Isola E1- Centro Direzionale, 80143 Napoli, Italy (professional representative) 

a g a i n s t

Antonio Viani Importe GmbH, August-Spindler-Straße 12, 37079 Göttingen, Germany (applicant), represented by Rehberg Hüppe + Partner Patentanwälte Partg mbB, Robert-Gernhardt-Platz 1, 37073 Göttingen, Germany (professional representative).

On 30/07/2026, the Opposition Division takes the following

DECISION:

REASONS

On 21/12/2023, the opponent filed an opposition against all the goods of European Union trade mark application No 18 893 642  (figurative mark), namely all the goods in Classes 18, 25, 29 and 30. 

During the opposition procedure, the examination of the absolute grounds was reopened, and the EUTM application was partially refused on Articles 7(1)(b) and (c) EUTMR. Following this partial refusal, the Opposition Division notified the opponent thereof and invited it to confirm whether the opposition was maintained. The opponent confirmed that it maintained the opposition against all the remaining goods in Classes 18 and 25, namely:

Class 18: Luggage, bags, wallets and other carriers, umbrellas and parasols, coats for animals.

Class 25: Clothing, headgear, footwear, parts of clothing, footwear and headgear.

The opposition is based on PDO ‘POMODORO SAN ‎MARZANO DELL'AGRO SARNESE-NOCERINO’ protected for ‘tomatoes’. The opponent invoked Article 8(6) EUTMR.

PRELIMINARY REMARK ON THE APPLICABLE REGULATION

The present case concerns the application of Regulation (EU) 1151/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 November 2012 on quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuffs.

The Opposition Division notes that the abovementioned Regulation was repealed by Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on geographical indications for wine, spirit drinks and agricultural products, as well as traditional specialities guaranteed and optional quality terms for agricultural products, amending Regulations (EU) No 1308/2013, (EU) 2019/787 and (EU) 2019/1753 and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 (hereinafter Regulation (EU) 2024/1143). 

According to Article 97 of Regulation 2024/1143 (‘Entry into force and date of application’), the Regulation applies from 13/05/2024. Moreover, according to established case-law, the decisive date for the purpose of identifying the applicable substantive law is the filling date of the contested trade mark. Given that the contested trade mark in this case was filed before 13/05/2024, the applicable Regulation at the time of filing the opposition was Regulation (EU) 1151/2012 and the present decision will, therefore, only refer to the provisions set out therein.

DESIGNATIONS OF ORIGIN OR GEOGRAPHICAL INDICATIONS — ARTICLE 8(6) EUTMR

According to Article 8(6) EUTMR, upon opposition by any person authorised under the relevant law to exercise the rights arising from a designation of origin or a geographical indication, the trade mark applied for must not be registered where and to the extent that, pursuant to the Union legislation or national law providing for the protection of designations of origin or geographical indications:

(i)   an application for a designation of origin or a geographical indication had already been submitted, in accordance with Union legislation or national law, prior to the date of application for registration of the EU trade mark or the date of the priority claimed for the application, subject to its subsequent registration;

(ii)   that designation of origin or geographical indication confers the right to prohibit the use of a subsequent trade mark.

a) The earlier right and the opponent’s entitlement to file the opposition

The opposition is based on the Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) ‘POMODORO SAN ‎MARZANO DELL'AGRO SARNESE-NOCERINO’ for tomatoes.

The contested mark was filed on 27/06/2023. Therefore, in order to substantiate this right, the opponent was required to prove that the invoked right was acquired prior to that date. 

Moreover, the opponent must prove its entitlement to file the opposition, namely, that it is authorised under the relevant law to exercise the rights arising from a GI (Article 46(1)(d) EUTMR and Article 7(2) EUTMDR). Furthermore, the opponent must prove that the applicable law confers on it a direct right of action to prohibit unlawful use of a GI. 

In order to substantiate this earlier right, the opponent relied on, inter alia:

- an extract confirming the registration of the earlier PDO, from the Register of Protected Designation of Origin and Protected Geographical Indications (Annex C). According to this document, the PDO ‘at issue has been registered since 02/07/1996 under the file number PDO-IT-1524. 

- Commission Implementing Decision of 8 April 2019, on the publication in the Official Journal of the European Union of the application for approval of an amendment, which is not minor, to a product specification referred to in Article 53 of Regulation (EU) no. 1151/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council for the name ‘Pomodoro S. Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese-Nocerino’ (PDO) (Annex D), according to which:

‘The name ‘Pomodoro S. Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese-Nocerino’ has been replaced by ‘Pomodoro San Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese-Nocerino’. The amendment request is justified by the need to correct a transcription error, in the Union Register, of the term ‘S. Marzano’. (…) The registered indication of the protected designation, namely ‘Pomodoro S. Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese Nocerino’, is likely to mislead the consumer because of the marketing of plant varieties registered under names such as ‘S. Marzano 2’ (synonyms: ‘S. Marzano Vesuvio 2’ and ‘S. Marzano lampadina 2’), ‘S. Marzano 3’ (synonyms: ‘S. Marzano Vesuvio 3’ and ‘S. Marzano lampadina 3’), ‘S. Marzano gigante 2’ and ‘S. Marzano gigante 3’. Moreover, as can be seen from the historical documentation presented in 1996 at the time of the request for registration, (…), the historical and traditional name used to identify the product has always been ‘Pomodoro San Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese-Nocerino’. 

- Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1346 of 8 August 2019 approving non-minor amendments to the specification for a name entered in the register of Protected Designations of Origin and protected Geographical Indications (Annex H) which stated that the amendments to the specification published in the Official Journal of the European Union regarding the PDO ‘Pomodoro San Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese-Nocerino’ are hereby approved. (Annex H)

Consequently, it is concluded that the opponent has proven the acquisition, continued existence and scope of protection of the PDO ‘POMODORO SAN ‎MARZANO DELL'AGRO SARNESE-NOCERINO’ prior to the filing of the contested mark.

As regards the opponent’s legal standing, the opponent submitted, inter alia, the following documents within the substantiation period:

- Article 14, paragraph 15, of Law no. 526 of 21 December 1999 establishes, inter alia, that the Consorzio for the protection of PDO "have functions of protection, promotion, enhancement, consumer information and general care of the interests relating to the designation of origin" and that they "collaborate, according to the directives issued by the Ministry of Agricultural and Forestry Policies, in the supervision, protection and safeguarding of the PDO […]from abuse, acts of unfair competition, counterfeiting, improper use of the protected names and behavior that is in any case prohibited by law; this activity is carried out at every level and towards anyone, in every phase of production, transformation and trade" (mentioned in the opponent’s observations of 21/12/2023).

- Ministerial Decree of December 4, 2003, published in the Official Gazette of the Italian Republic no.293 of 18.12.2003, according to which ‘1. The Consorzio San Marzano Consortium for the valorisation and protection of the PDO ‘Pomodoro San Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese-Nocerino’ is recognized pursuant to art. 14, paragraph 15 of law 21 December 1999, n. 526, and is responsible for carrying out the functions envisaged by the same paragraph, on the PDO ‘Pomodoro San Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese-Nocerino’ registered with regulation (EC) no. 1263 of the Commission of 1 July 1996.

- Copy of the Ministerial decree of November 24, 2022, published in the Official Gazette of the Italian Republic - General series no. 285 - of 06.12.2022 (Annex 1 and 2) confirming the assignment to the Consorzio di tutela del Pomodoro San Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese- Nocerino DOP to carry out the functions referred to in article 53 of law 24 April 1998, n. 128, as amended by article 14, paragraph 15, of law 21 December 1999, n. 526, for the PDO ‘POMODORO SAN MARZANO DELL'AGRO SARNESE-NOCERINO'. 

Based on the documents listed above, it is concluded that, at the date set by the Office for substantiating its earlier rights, the opponent has provided sufficient evidence as to its entitlement to exercise the rights arising from the earlier PDO, and, in particular, to file the present opposition.

b) The right under applicable law

Designations of origin and geographical indications protected under Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 November 2012 on quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuffs as amended by Regulation (EU) 2021/2117 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 2 December 2021 amending Regulations (EU) No 1308/2013 establishing a common organisation of the markets in agricultural products, (EU) No 1151/2012 on quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuffs, (EU) No 251/2014 on the definition, description, presentation, labelling and the protection of geographical indications of aromatised wine products and (EU) No 228/2013 laying down specific measures for agriculture in the outermost regions of the Union (hereinafter Regulation No 1151/2012), fall under Article 8(6) EUTMR.

According to Article 5(1) of Regulation No 1151/2012, ‘designation of origin’ is a name, which may be a traditionally used name, which identifies a product:

	originating in a specific place, region or, in exceptional cases, country;

	whose quality or characteristics are essentially or exclusively due to a particular geographical environment with its inherent natural and human factors; and

	the production steps of which all take place in the defined geographical area.

According to Article 13(1) of Regulation No 1151/2012, registered names will be protected against:

(a)	any direct or indirect commercial use of a registered name in respect of products not covered by the registration where those products are comparable to the products registered under that name or where using the name exploits, weakens or dilutes the reputation of the protected name, including when those products are used as an ingredient;

(b)	any misuse, imitation or evocation, even if the true origin of the products or services is indicated or if the protected name is translated or accompanied by an expression such as ‘style’, ‘type’, ‘method’, ‘as produced in’, ‘imitation’ or similar, including when those products are used as an ingredient;

(c)	any other false or misleading indication as to the provenance, origin, nature or essential qualities of the product that is used on the inner or outer packaging, advertising material or documents relating to the product concerned, and the packing of the product in a container liable to convey a false impression as to its origin;

(d)	any other practice liable to mislead the consumer as to the true origin of the product.

Where a protected designation of origin or a protected geographical indication contains within it the name of a product that is considered to be generic, the use of that generic name will not be considered to be contrary to points (a) or (b) of the first subparagraph.

It follows from the above that a contested EUTM application must be refused pursuant to Article 8(6) EUMTR in conjunction with the above provisions, where any of the situations referred to in Article 13(1) of Regulation No 1151/2012 would occur.

c) The opponent’s right vis-à-vis the contested trade mark

It is to be recalled that the earlier PDO and the contested sign are the following:

The relevant territory is European Union.

The earlier PDO enjoys protection for tomatoes, while the opposition is directed against the following goods:

Class 25: Clothing, headgear, footwear, parts of clothing, footwear and headgear.

Class 18: Luggage, bags, wallets and other carriers, umbrellas and parasols, coats for animals.

The opponent referred and cited in its observations the above mentioned article 13(1) of Regulation No 1151/2012 as well as article 14(1) of the cited regulation according to which ‘Where a designation of origin or a geographical indication is registered under this Regulation, the registration of a trade mark the use of which would contravene Article 13(1) and which relates to a product of the same type shall be refused if the application for registration of the trade mark is submitted after the date of submission of the registration application in respect of the designation of origin or the geographical indication to the Commission. Trade marks registered in breach of the first subparagraph shall be invalidated’.

Moreover, the Opponent’s arguments concerning the alleged infringement of the PDO by the contested sign, as regards the abovementioned limited list of goods covered by the contested sign, are summarised below:

- The contested mark includes ‘SAN MARZANO’ which is a constitutive element of the PDO ‘POMODORO SAN MARZANO DELL'AGRO SARNESE-NOCERINO’, in combination with the ‘No.2’ that recalls the PDO as the number of the plant variety S. Marzano (as well as Kiros) relating to the present case. 

- Furthermore, the pictogram of the bunch of tomatoes included in the contested EUTMA strengthens the intent to evoke the PDO which has also the same pictogram in the logo approved by the Commission to distinguish products compliant with the product Specifications.

- The use of the contested EUTMA for each good other than identical or similar ones of the PDO, will evoke in the consumer mind the PDO involving them, especially when the goods, of any kind, edible or not, are sold in the same stores (physical and/or virtual). The consumer could be attracted by any good that shows or evoke a PDO, associating their prestige, reputation and quality in support of the excellence undoubtedly represented by a PDO and whose registration is subjected to the examination according national and community law provisions in addition to the checks required by law. 

- PDOs and PGls are not only protected against direct or indirect commercial use, but also against other situations that exploit and damage the image of PDOs and PGls. The contested EUTMA is clearly aurally, phonetically, visually, and conceptually similar to the PDO 'POMODORO SAN MARZANO DELL'AGRO SARNESE-NOCERINO’. This leads, i.a. to evocation.

- The remaining contested goods in Classes 18 and 25 can be associated by relevant consumer with the PDO and, consequently, he can therefore be misled about for example the origin of the product.

- The wording of the contested EUTMA ‘SAN MARZANO No. 2’, reproduces the important element of the PDO (different to the plant variety name - see Annex l) in combination with the pictogram very similar of the PDO’s logo and the element ‘no.2’ of the plant variety related the protected good. Consequently, the EUTMA is highly similar from a visual, phonetic and conceptual point of view to the protected name. In view of the above and according to case law, there is direct commercial use of the element belonging the PDO of the present case, there is an evocation and also an exploitation of the reputation.

- The PDO enjoys, due to its recognition and registration as PDO, an objective reputation, which must be taken into consideration by the Office without need of evidence. 

- the Applicant is trying to take the benefits of the PDO, with the aim of transferring the reputation and aura of quality, of which this PDO enjoys, from 'POMODORO SAN MARZANO DELL'AGRO SARNESE-NOCERINO’ to its goods. 

- The relevant consumer in front of the goods ‘SAN MARZANO No.2’ may believe that those goods have the qualities and characteristics of the PDO "POMODORO SAN MARZANO DELL'AGRO SARNESE-NOCERINO" goods.

- Evocation can be established either with respect to contested signs used on comparable products with respect to the ones of the PDO, PGI or Gl at issue (absolute protection) as well as with respect to other goods and services which are not comparable (if the contested sign exploits the reputation of the PDO, PGI or Gl at issue): The issue of evocation with respect to contested signs used on goods and services which are not comparable to the ones of the PDO at issue is dealt with by the CJEU in case C- 783/19 (the use of "Champanillo" as a business name for restaurants). ‘(…) the Court considers that the concept of 'evocation' does not require that the product covered by the PDO and the product or service covered by the disputed name be identical or similar. Evocation is established where the use of a name creates, in the mind of an average European consumer who is reasonably well informed and reasonably observant and circumspect, a sufficiently clear and direct link between (that) name and the PDO’.

It follows from the above that the opponent invokes Article 8(6) EUTMR in relation, in particular, to the infringement of Article 13(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation No 1151/2012. The Opposition Division will now examine whether the conditions set out in the above provisions are met vis-à-vis the contested trade mark. 

The main line of defence of the applicant is that the non-geographical part ‘Pomodoro San Marzano’ or ‘San Marzano’, does not enjoy protection on its own, because the protected name is ‘Pomodoro San Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese-Nocerino’. Consequently, the use of the name ‘San Marzano’ in contested EUTM application does not infringe the protection granted to the PDO by the relevant Regulation.

Issue of ‘S. Marzano’ plant variety: 

- The opponent argues that in the Register of Plant Varieties, kept by the Italian Ministry of Agricultural Policy, there are plant varieties relating to the tomatoes referred to in the product Specification of the PDO of the present case, registered as S. Marzano 2 and Kiros plant varieties (Annex I and Annex L). 

- According to the opponent, this aspect is particularly important as well as diriment in the present case, since the contested mark reproduces the expression ‘San Marzano’ rather than ‘S. Marzano’. While the latter designates a plant variety, the former refers to specific goods enjoying certified quality and an established reputation. 

- In this context, the opponent submits evidence of the approved request to change of the PDO name from the ‘Pomodoro S. Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese-Nocerino’ to ‘Pomodoro San Marzano dell'Agro Sarnese-Nocerino’ which determined the amendment approved by the Commission in 2019 (Annex D and Annex H).

- The applicant claims that the distinction made between San Marzano and S. Marzano is not convincing since i) ‘S.’ is a common Italian abbreviation for San, ii) from an internet search it is clear that San Marzano refers to both ‘S. Marzano’ and ‘San Marzano’ tomatoes, iii) the name of the consortium applying for the PDO at issue is ‘Consorzio di Tutela del pomodoro S. Marzano dell’Agro Sarnese Nocerino’. The applicant also submits an official statement from the Italian Minister of Agricolture, Food and Forestry confirming the applicant’s position, namely that since ‘San Marzano’ is the name of a plant variety and not a protected designation of origin, it may be freely incorporated into the trade marks of undertakings marketing tomatoes of that variety.

- In reply to this, the opponent submits the correspondence received through ORIGIN (Organisation for an International Geographical Indications Network), between the ‘Ispettorato centrale della tutela della qualità e repressione frodi dei prodotti agroalimentari’ -- ICQRF - and the German authorities, regarding the improper use of ‘San Marzano’ from the applicant for S. Marzano variety tomatoes that do not comply with the PDO at issue. Moreover, the opponent also submits a screenshot from the Italian Official Register of Vegetable, Plant Varieties of the Ministry of Agricultural, Food and Forestry Policies showing that registered tomatoes varieties in 2014 are S. Marzano 2., S. Marzano 3, S. Marzano gigante 2 and S. Marzano gigante 3.

Use, including exploitation of the reputation of the GI – Article 13(1)(a) of Regulation No 1151/2012

Article 13(1)(a) of Regulation No 1151/2012 grants protection in respect of any direct or indirect commercial use of a registered name in respect of products not covered by the registration where those products are comparable to the products registered under that name or where using the name exploits the reputation of the protected name, including where those products are used as an ingredient.

The notion of use

As a preliminary remark, ‘direct and indirect use’ need to be defined/interpreted. According to the Court (07/06/2018, C-44/17, SCOTCH WHISKY, EU:C:2018:415, § 32), direct and indirect use merely refer to the physical manner in which the use of a protected geographical indication or protected designation of origin (hereinafter ‘GI’) appears on the market: ‘direct use’ implies that the GI is affixed directly to the product or its packaging, while ‘indirect use’ requires the GI to feature in supplementary marketing or information sources, such as an advertisement for the product or documents relating to it. This distinction plays no role for the assessment of the opposition, as the Opposition Division is not concerned with the subsequent placing on the market of the mark proposed for registration.

According to the Court, ‘the word “use” … requires, by definition, that the sign at issue makes use of the protected geographical indication itself, in the form in which that indication was registered or, at least, in a form with such close links to it, in visual and/or phonetic terms, that the sign at issue clearly cannot be dissociated from it’ (07/06/2018, C-44/17, SCOTCH WHISKY, EU:C:2018:415, § 29; 09/09/2021, C-783/19, Champanillo, EU:C:2021:713, § 38).

The Court has further emphasized that the concept of use must be interpreted in a strict manner so the concept of ‘evocation’ is not deprived of its usefulness, which would be contrary to the intention of the EU legislator (09/09/2021, C-783/19, Champanillo, EU:C:2021:713, § 40).

In addition, there must be a logical separation of the GI from the rest of the term for it to be identifiable. In other words, there will not be use when a trade mark contains the GI as part of a word element that does not bring to the consumer’s mind the product whose designation is protected. This is normally the case when the term has its own meaning.

In the present case, the verbal element of the contested sign is ‘SAN MARZANO No. 2’ whereas the earlier PDO is ‘POMODORO SAN MARZANO DELL'AGRO SARNESE-NOCERINO. Since the contested sign reproduces only a part of the earlier PDO, it cannot be considered to be so close to the earlier PDO that the sign at issue could not be dissociated from it (as per 07/06/2018, C-44/17, SCOTCH WHISKY, EU:C:2018:415, § 29; 09/09/2021, C-783/19, Champanillo, EU:C:2021:713, § 38). 

Consequently, there is no direct commercial use of the earlier PDO in the contested sign. 

The notion of comparable products

The notion of comparable products must be understood in a restrictive sense, and it is independent from the ‘Canon criteria’. According to case-law, products are ‘comparable’ when they have common objective characteristics, such as the method of elaboration, the physical appearance of the product and the use of the same raw materials. Other factors that may be relevant are, from the perspective of the relevant public, the consumption on identical occasions and the identical channels of distribution and marketing methods (14/07/2011, C-4/10 & C-27/10, BNI Cognac, EU:C:2011:484, § 54; Article 16(a) of Regulation (EC) No 110/2008).

In addition, factors such as whether the products are consumed, from the point of view of the relevant public, on largely identical occasions, or whether they are distributed through the same channels and/or subject to similar marketing rules, can be taken into account in order to confirm whether goods are comparable.

The contested goods in Classes 18 and 25 are clothing, footwear, headgear and parts thereof, as well as luggage, bags, wallets, other carriers, umbrellas, parasols and coats for animals. Their nature is very different from tomatoes protected by the PDO. These goods and tomatoes not only are not comparable, but belong to very distant fields, address different consumer needs, are not intended for the same uses or occasions, and are normally developed, manufactured and marketed by unrelated undertakings.

Consequently, the is no direct commercial use of the earlier PDO in the contested sign and, moreover, none of the contested goods are comparable to tomatoes protected by the earlier PDO. Therefore, the claim based on Article 13(1)(a) of Regulation No 1151/2012 must be rejected as unfounded. 

Reputation of the PDO

For sake of completeness, the Opposition Division will now consider if other conditions of the second alternative of Article 13(1)(a) of Regulation No 1151/2012 are met, to see whether the use of the contested sign exploits, weakens or dilutes the reputation of the protected PDO, including when those products are used as an ingredient. 

The applicable rules protect those entitled to use designations of origin against improper use of those designations by third parties seeking to profit from the reputation which the products, bearing a geographical indication registered by virtue of the relevant Regulations, have acquired by their quality. They are intended to guarantee that the product bearing them comes from a specified geographical area and displays certain particular characteristics. 

The reputation of GIs depends on their image in the minds of consumers, and that image, in turn, depends essentially on particular characteristics and more generally on the quality of the product. It is on the quality of the product that its reputation is based (14/09/2017, C-56/16 P, PORT CHARLOTTE, EU:C:2017:693, § 81-82). Therefore, contrary to the situation with trade marks, where reputation is quantitatively assessed, the reputation of a geographical indication is linked only to the quality of the product that it designates. All registered geographical indications offer a guarantee of quality due to their geographical provenance. Therefore, the Office considers that GIs are intrinsically reputed within the meaning of Article 13(1)(a) of Regulation No 1151/2012 by the mere fact that they are registered. This is irrespective of whether a GI has been registered based on a claim in the application to its reputation being essentially attributable to its geographical origin Article 5(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012.

In this regard, as also stated by the opponent, the Opposition Division notes that opponents do not have to submit evidence of the reputation of the GI. Nevertheless, opponents must submit convincing arguments and/or evidence regarding the exploitation, weakening, dilution or detriment to the reputation of the GI as well as the notoriety of the GI on the market if that is a factor that the opponent considers relevant. 

The Court held that ‘[t]he incorporation in a trade mark of a name which is protected … cannot be held to be capable of exploiting the reputation of that [name] … if that incorporation does not lead the relevant public to associate that mark or the goods in respect of which it is registered with the [name] concerned or the … product in respect of which it is protected’ (14/09/2017, C-56/16 P, PORT CHARLOTTE, EU:C:2017:693, § 115). 

As a rule, general allegations (such as merely citing the relevant wording of the EU regulations) of exploitation of the reputation will not be sufficient in themselves for proving such exploitation: the opponent must adduce evidence and/or develop a cogent line of argument, taking into account both rights, the goods and services in question and all the relevant circumstances, to demonstrate specifically how the alleged injury might occur.

The opponent has not submitted any evidence on the reputation of the earlier PDO, nor any convincing arguments regarding taking of unfair advantage, exploiting, weakening or diluting the reputation of the earlier PDO. 

Article 95(1) EUTMR requires the opponent to submit and prove all the facts on which its opposition is based. In discharging this burden of proof, the opponent cannot merely contend that exploitation of the reputation would be a necessary consequence flowing automatically from the use of the sign applied for, owing to the strong reputation and image of the earlier GI. 

The European system for the protection of geographical indications does not provide automatic or blanket protection against possible use of the protected designation for any goods or services, without providing convincing evidence or – at least – reasoned argumentation regarding the existence of the risks provided in the respective legislation. 

This principle was confirmed in a recent judgment of the General Court in case 26/02/2025, T-23/24, Quevedo Port, EU:T:2025:182, where the Court upheld the Board’s finding regarding the lack of exploitation of reputation of the PDO ‘Port’ in the mark ‘Quevedo Port’ applied for olive oil in Class 29, taking into account the lack of convincing arguments or evidence to the contrary.

The Court stated:

58      Lastly, it must be found that none of the arguments submitted by the applicant can call into question the finding made by the Board of Appeal in the contested decision that the applicant ‘failed to adduce evidence [or] at least develop a coherent line of argument to demonstrate specifically how the use of the contested sign, that seeks protection for olive oils in Class 29, would result in exploitation of the reputation of the [name] “Port” [of the earlier PDO] protected for wine’.

59      As in the proceedings before EUIPO (see paragraph 38 of the contested decision), the applicant merely makes general statements regarding the similarity of the signs at issue and the fact that there is, in its view, almost automatic exploitation of the reputation of the earlier PDO and its image irrespective of the nature of the products concerned.

(…)

62     (…) By contrast, it did not develop any specific arguments capable of calling into question the reasoning of the Board of Appeal as regards, in particular, the way in which the use of the contested sign, that seeks protection for olive oils in Class 29, would result in exploitation of the reputation of the name ‘Port’ of the earlier PDO protected for wine.

The same reasoning was adopted by the General Court in case 26/02/2025, T-40/24, Portsoy, EU:T:2025:183, concerning the lack of exploitation of reputation of the PDO ‘Port’ in the trade mark ‘Portsoy’ applied for Scotch Whisky complying with the specifications of the PGI Scotch Whisky in Class 33:

80      Accordingly, contrary to what the applicant claims and for the reasons stated previously, it seems unlikely that the mere incorporation of the element ‘port’ in the contested sign in order to designate whisky would be sufficient to establish an association between the contested sign and the name ‘Port’ used by the earlier PDO to protect wines based on their quality and geographical provenance.

81      Lastly, and in any event, it must be found that none of the arguments submitted by the applicant can call into question the finding of the Board of Appeal in the contested decision that the applicant ‘failed to adduce evidence and/or at least develop a coherent line of argument to demonstrate specifically how, taking into account the signs and all the relevant circumstances, the use of the contested sign in relation to the non-comparable goods would result in exploitation of the reputation of the earlier PDO …’.

82      The applicant merely makes general statements regarding the similarity of the signs at issue and the fact that there is, in its view, almost automatic exploitation of the reputation of the earlier PDO and its image irrespective of the nature of the products concerned.

(…)

85    (…) By contrast, it did not develop any specific arguments capable of calling into question the reasoning of the Board of Appeal as regards, in particular, the way in which the use of the contested sign to designate products which were not comparable would result in exploitation of the reputation of the earlier PDO.

Therefore, irrespective of the fact that there is no direct commercial use of the earlier PDO in the contested sign, the Opposition Division concludes that the opponent did not sufficiently demonstrate how the use of the contested trade mark, given the type of the products under comparison, would give rise to a risk of exploitation of the reputation of the earlier PDO. Despite some visual and phonetic similarities between the earlier PDO and the contested sign share, this is very unlikely, since the contested goods and the goods protected by the earlier PDO belong to very distant fields, address different consumer needs, are not intended for the same uses or occasions, and are normally developed, manufactured and marketed by unrelated undertakings. 

Therefore, the claim under Article 13(1)(a) of Regulation No 1151/2012 must be dismissed.

Article 13(1)(b) of Regulation No 1151/2012 – Misuse, imitation or evocation of a GI

Article 13(1)(b) of Regulation No 1151/2012 grants protection in respect of any misuse, imitation or evocation, even if the true origin of the products or services is indicated or if the protected name is translated, transcripted or transliterated or accompanied by an expression such as ‘style’, ‘type’, ‘method’, etc., including when those products are used as an ingredient.

Neither the EUTMR nor the EU regulations define the meaning of ‘misuse’, ‘imitation’ or ‘evocation’.

In the absence of any guidance from the Court, the Office considers that an EUTM ‘misuses’ a GI when it provides false indications as to the geographical source of the goods, with the result that it benefits from the perceived quality of the GI.

The mark ‘imitates’ (mimics, reproduces elements of, etc.), with the result that the product designated by the GI is ‘evoked’ (called to mind). The term ‘evocation’ requires less than ‘imitation’ or ‘misuse’ (Advocate General - 04/03/1999, C-87/97, Cambozola, EU:C:1998:614, § 33). Nevertheless, the Office considers the terms ‘imitation’ and ‘evocation’ as two corollaries of essentially the same concept.

Moreover, there is ‘imitation’, in the common meaning of the term, where the trade mark is ‘intended to simulate or copy something else’, here the earlier GI (30/11/2018, R 0251/2016-1, COLOMBIANO COFFEE HOUSE (fig.), § 135). By contrast, ‘evocation’ is objective. For its application there is no need to show that the owner of the mark intended to evoke the earlier GI or that any fault existed (Advocate General - 04/03/1999, C-87/97, Cambozola, EU:C:1998:614, § 33; 09/09/2021, C-783/19, Champanillo, EU:C:2021:713, § 68).

According to the Court, the decisive criterion for finding ‘evocation’ is whether, ‘when the consumer is confronted with a disputed designation, the image triggered directly in his mind is that of the product whose geographical indication is protected’ (07/06/2018, C-44/17, SCOTCH WHISKY, EU:C:2018:415, § 51; 04/03/1999, C-87/97, Cambozola, EU:C:1999:115, § 25; 26/02/2008, C-132/05, Parmigiano Reggiano, EU:C:2008:117, § 44; 21/01/2016, C-75/15, Viiniverla, EU:C:2016:35, § 21; 09/09/2021, C-783/19, Champanillo, EU:C:2021:713, § 58). 

Consumers must establish a sufficiently clear and direct link between the term used to designate the product and the product whose name is protected (21/01/2016, C-75/15, Viiniverla, EU:C:2016:35, § 22; 07/06/2018, C-44/17, SCOTCH WHISKY, EU:C:2018:415, § 53; 09/09/2021, C-783/19, Champanillo, EU:C:2021:713, § 59). 

At the same time, it is necessary to take account of the presumed expectation of the average consumer, who is reasonably well informed and reasonably observant and circumspect (26/02/2008, C-132/05, Parmigiano Reggiano, EU:C:2008:117, § 44; 04/03/1999, C-87/97, Cambozola, EU:C:1999:115, § 25; 07/06/2018, C-44/17, Scotch Whisky, EU:C:2018:415, § 46 y 47; 21/01/2016, C-75/15, Verlados / Calvados, EU:C:2016:35, § 25, 28). In particular, it is not enough if the term incorporated in the trade mark application evokes in the relevant public some kind of association with the protected geographical indication or the area relating thereto, because such association does not necessarily establish a sufficiently clear and direct link between that element and the indication concerned (07/06/2018, C-44/17, SCOTCH WHISKY, EU:C:2018:415, § 53).

EU Regulations protect GIs throughout the territory of the European Union. As a result, the Court has ruled that in order to guarantee effective and uniform protection of those GIs in that territory, it must be considered that the concept of the consumer covers European consumers and not merely consumers of the Member State in which the product giving rise to the evocation of the GI is manufactured (21/01/2016, C-75/15, Viiniverla, EU:C:2016:35, § 27; 07/06/2018, C-44/17, SCOTCH WHISKY, EU:C:2018:415, § 59; 09/09/2021, C-783/19, Champanillo, EU:C:2021:713, § 62-63). In this respect, while the effective and uniform protection of registered names means that circumstances which may lead to the conclusion that there is no ‘evocation’ only in respect of the consumers of one Member State must be disregarded, that does not mean, on the other hand, that evocation assessed by reference to the consumers of a single Member State is not sufficient to trigger the protection provided in Article 13(1)(b) of Regulation No 1151/2012 (02/05/2019, C-614/17, queso manchego, EU:C:2019:344, § 48).

As clarified by the Court, the existence of a link between the signs may result from several elements, in particular, the partial incorporation of the protected designation, phonetic and visual similarity between the two designations and the resulting similarity, and even, in the absence of those elements, from the conceptual similarity between the PDO and the designation at issue and also from a similarity between the products covered by that PDO and the goods or services covered by that designation (09/09/2021, C-783/19, Champanillo, EU:C:2021:713, § 66).

The Court of Justice has also clarified, as also noted by the opponent, that the concept of ‘evocation’ extends to all uses which take unfair advantage of the reputation enjoyed by the GI through association with it (C-783/19, Champanillo § 50, see also the Opinion of the Advocate General Pitruzzella of 29/04/2021, C-783/19, Champanillo, § 36-37).

In the Opposition Division’s view, there will be no evocation of the earlier PDO concerning the contested goods in Classes 18 and 25. As seen above, these goods are very distant from tomatoes protected by the earlier PDO. Indeed, they belong to very distinct sectors (fashion, footwear, and leather goods sector v agrifood), address different segments of consumers and cater for different needs. 

In this regard, it is worth noting that the protection conferred by the relevant GI Regulation extends to the protected GI name and prohibits any evocation of the product covered by that GI. An evocation based on a figurative element is not excluded, provided that, when used in relation to the goods at issue, it directly brings to the mind of the relevant consumer the product covered by the protected GI. Moreover, such an association must be sufficiently clear and direct.

The line of argumentation provided by the opponent is indeed very poor in connection to goods in Classes 18 and 25, as the opponent does not argue why there should be evocation in this case merely mentioning that there may be evocation based on incorporation of part of the GI and on figurative elements of the contested sign. Furthermore, it refers to CJEU in case C- 783/19, according to which the concept of 'evocation' does not require that the product covered by the PDO and the product or service covered by the disputed name be identical or similar. However, the opponent fails to provide any further case-specific reasoning or evidence explaining how that principle applies to the present case.

Indeed, in this case the contested mark does not reproduce the entire PDO or at least its geographical part ‘DELL'AGRO SARNESE-NOCERINO’, it merely reproduces the element ‘San Marzano’. The opponent has not shown that San Marzano-type tomatoes or protected plant variety ‘S. Marzano 2’ are exclusively linked with the invoked PDO in the consumer’s mind. In this regard, it is worth noting that the evidence submitted by the opponent does not demonstrate that the relevant public — in particular consumers purchasing clothing or leather goods — is aware of the distinction between ‘San Marzano’ and ‘S. Marzano’, or, more importantly, that the former is associated with the PDO whereas the latter refers to the plant variety. In fact, both this plant variety and the traditional ‘San Marzano’ varieties of tomatoes are used by producers in different areas of the European Union. Moreover, while the protection of plant varieties is relevant for goods in Class 31 it is unrelated to goods in Classes 18 and 25. 

In the context of the fashion industry, the debate as to whether ‘San Marzano’ or ‘S. Marzano’ refers to the PDO or to a particular tomato variety is of limited relevance. Indeed, the relevant consumers of clothing, headgear, footwear in Class 25 and other goods in Class 18 are not specialists in plant varieties and are unlikely to engage in such an analysis. Rather, part of the Italian public, or, more generally, the public familiar with ‘San Marzano’ or ‘S. Marzano’ tomatoes, may recognise the verbal element ‘San Marzano’ followed by the ‘No. 2’, and the figurative representation of tomatoes represented in the contested sign as a reference to a type of tomato represented also as a decorative feature, when encountering the contested sign in relation to fashion and leather goods in Classes 18 and 25. However, such recognition does not, in itself, mean that those consumers will establish a link between the sign and the protected geographical indication.

As regards the remaining relevant public, which might not attribute any particular meaning to the term ‘San Marzano’, the contested sign is even more likely to be perceived merely as a decorative reference to tomatoes, in view of the figurative element depicting tomatoes, without any association being made with the protected geographical indication. Accordingly, the contested sign is not capable of giving rise, in the mind of the average consumer, to a sufficiently direct and unequivocal mental link with the protected geographical indication.

In fact, considering the goods in question, even if the public were to perceive ‘San Marzano’ as a type of tomato, it would be as the general concept of a kind of tomato, rather than any particular tomato connected with a PDO.

As to the pictogram of the contested sign, it is a rather generic image representing a cluster of tomatoes which is not the same as the one in the logo of the PDO. In any case, it is unlikely that the relevant consumer should be aware of the logo of the PDO from such a different sector.

As a result, it is unlikely that the affixing of a such an image on a fashion article would be linked to the mentioned PDO, even if it is accompanied by the words ‘San Marzano’ or by ‘No. 2’. 

It is common in the fashion industry to use names and images of fruit and vegetables, so it is the likely scenario that the consumer when perceiving the image of tomatoes accompanied by ‘San Marzano’ will perceive them as such, namely as referring to the generic concept of tomatoes or a kind of tomatoes, and thus as a fanciful connotation in the context of the fashion articles like clothing, footwear or handbags etc., but without any link to the invoked PDO.

As explained above, the opponent claimed that the PDO had intrinsic reputation, but such reputation is linked to the product which is covered by the GI, namely tomatoes, and the opponent has not provided any evidence or arguments to show how it could contribute to the evocation of the GI product in a trade mark pertaining to the fashion industry. The opponent also failed to provide any evidence of notoriety of a GI going beyond the intrinsic reputation which would support such conclusion. Moreover, the opponent failed to provide any convincing arguments, not to mention evidence, as to why the image triggered in the mind of the relevant public, when faced with the goods bearing the contested mark, would be that of the PDO in question. 

As a result, the evocation of the product covered by PDO ‘POMODORO SAN MARZANO DELL'AGRO SARNESE-NOCERINO’ by the contested trade mark can be excluded.

In view of all the foregoing, even taking into account the intrinsic reputation of the PDO, the lack of sound evidence and argumentation in general, cannot lead to any other conclusion.

Therefore, the claim under Article 13(1)(b) of Regulation No 1151/2012 must be dismissed.

False or misleading indication of origin and other practice liable to mislead the consumer

According to Article 13(1)(c) and(d) of Regulation No 1151/2012, registered names shall be protected against any other false or misleading indication as to the provenance, origin, nature or essential qualities of the product that is used on the inner or outer packaging, advertising material or documents relating to the product concerned, and the packing of the product in a container liable to convey a false impression as to its origin, as well as any  other practice liable to mislead the consumer as to the true origin of the product.

Points (c) and (d) of Article 13(1) of Regulation No 1151/2012 include any other indication that, while not actually evoking the protected geographical indication, is ‘false or misleading’ as regards the links between the product concerned and that indication (07/06/2018, C-44/17, Glen Buchenbach, EU:C:2018:415, § 65). These recitals cover situations where the reference to a protected geographical indication is even more subtle than an ‘evocation’ of that indication. For the purposes of points (c) and (d), it may suffice that the consumer would make an association of any kind whatsoever with a protected geographical indication (07/06/2018, C-44/17, Glen Buchenbach, EU:C:2018:415, § 53-54).

Account must be taken of the presumed expectations of the average consumer, who is reasonably well informed and reasonably observant and circumspect. In this case, the consumer will not be misled or induced to believe, incorrectly, that the product has an origin, provenance or quality which are other than genuine.

Taking into account that good faith is assumed, the Opposition Division cannot conclude that the contested sign is likely to convey a false impression that could be associated with the products protected by the PDO (tomatoes), since the application covers goods that are not comparable to and far removed from tomatoes and that the average consumer would not believe to have the same origin or quality. 

Consequently, the opposition cannot succeed either on the basis of these provisions and forms of infringement indicated therein.

Overall conclusion

Considering all the above, the Opposition Division finds that the conditions of Article 8(6) EUTMR in connection with Article 13(1)(a), (b), (c) and (d) of Regulation No 1151/2012 are not fulfilled. 

Therefore, the opposition is not well founded under Article 8(6) EUTMR and must be rejected in its entirety.

COSTS

According to Article 109(1) EUTMR, the losing party in opposition proceedings must bear the fees and costs incurred by the other party.

Since the opponent is the losing party, it must bear the costs incurred by the applicant in the course of these proceedings.

According to Article 109(7) EUTMR and Article 18(1)(c)(i) EUTMIR, the costs to be paid to the applicant are the costs of representation, which are to be fixed on the basis of the maximum rate set therein.
